messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh was 22 when he first came in, a single South Eastern Asian man living alone in a small apartment and working as a UX designer in a busy downtown office where he spent most days alternating between Figma files, Slack messages, and long stretches at his monitor. The storm that changed things had struck his family’s coastal town the year before, while he was visiting relatives. What had begun as a heavy, unsettling wind had become a natural disaster in the span of an evening: water forcing its way into the streets, neighbors shouting from doorways, power failing, and the house where he was staying shuddering under the strain. Minh remembered the confusion of trying to move through waist-high water with his relatives, the shock of seeing familiar roads turned into currents, and the relentless smell and taste of brackish floodwater that seemed to get into everything. In the weeks afterward, he found that the memory returned in fragments that felt at once too vivid and strangely unreal. He would think about the night and feel as though the whole event belonged to someone else, so extreme and unbelievable that he had to pause and ask himself if it had actually happened to him. At other times there would be no clear picture at all, only a sudden rush of the same fear and helplessness he had felt during the flooding, as if his body recalled the event before his mind could assemble an image. More than once, when the memory broke through, he noticed the stale taste of floodwater in his mouth so distinctly that he would spit into the sink and rinse his mouth several times, unsettled by how closely his present body seemed to reach back into that night.

As months passed, Minh became increasingly aware of the way ordinary sensations could pull him back. A kink in his neck after a long day at his desk, the kind of ache he would once have ignored, now made him stop and worry that something was wrong with him. If he woke feeling physically unwell, even mildly tired or off, his attention would narrow immediately to the possibility that something bad was happening again, and he would spend time checking himself rather than settling into the day. In the office, where he sat through design critiques and client calls, he sometimes found that a discussion of emergency systems, maps, evacuation routes, or any trauma-related news story on a coworker’s screen could catch him off guard. A headline about another flood in a different country, or a passing comment about a storm, could make him go quiet and grip the edge of his desk until he could steady himself. He was careful not to say much when those moments happened. He worried that other people would not understand, and that what had happened to him had made him too different from everyone around him to explain easily.

That sense of difference deepened over time. Minh had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that ordinary friendliness could hide a lack of real understanding, and that even well-meaning questions often left him feeling exposed rather than comforted. At work he kept conversations focused on tasks and avoided mentioning the flood, not because he wanted to be secretive, but because he was increasingly certain that others could not hold the reality of it without turning away, minimizing it, or looking at him with the kind of awkward pity he found unbearable. He felt isolated and set apart in meetings, in after-work lunches, and even in casual messages from friends who had no trouble moving on to weekend plans. He would see their ease with ordinary life and feel that he no longer belonged anywhere in quite the same way. The disaster had left him with a private, unshareable knowledge, and he often found himself sitting alone in his apartment after work, aware that he had a steady job and a clean room and people around him in the city, yet still feeling as if he stood just outside the life other people were living.

He sought help when the disorientation and the body-based reminders became harder to ignore and he realized how much he had organized his days around trying not to be caught off guard. What brought him in was not only the fear that the memories might keep breaking in, but the growing loneliness of feeling unlike everyone else and unable to trust that others would truly see what he had lived through. What he most hoped for was a way to make sense of the event without feeling as though it belonged to someone else, and a way to move through his work and daily life without every neck ache, moment of feeling ill, or mention of a storm opening the same old wound.
